School library media programs help K-12 students become more academically competent.
Researchers from the Library Research Service of the Colorado State Library and the University of Denver conducted four statewide studies on the impact of school library media programs on academic achievement.
The studies include 'Information Empowered: The School Librarian as an Agent of Academic Achievement in Alaska', 'Measuring Up to Standards: The Impact of School Library Programs and Information Literacy in Pennsylvania Schools', 'How School Librarians Help Kids Achieve Standards, The Second Colorado Study', and 'Good Schools Have School Librarians: Oregon School Librarians Collaborate to Improve Academic Achievement'.
The studies are based on the 'Information Power' model from the American Association of School Librarians.
The latest edition of Information Power: Building Partnerships for Learning was published in 1998.
The 1998 edition identifies three roles for school library media specialists: advancing instructional goals, providing information access and delivery, and serving as program administrators.
Library media specialists develop collections and services and facilitate their use.
Library media specialists serve as library media center managers and advocates for information literacy.

The National Science Foundation (NSF) released its first call for proposals for the National Science, Mathematics, Engineering, and Technology Education Digital Library (NSDL) program in early 2000.
The NSDL program aims to establish a national digital library for science, mathematics, engineering, and technology education.
Fiscal year 1994 marked the beginning of the Digital Libraries Initiative (DLI), a multi-agency research effort involving NSF, NASA, and ARPA.
NSF served as the lead agency in the Digital Libraries Initiative (DLI).
The DLI provided support for basic research into the transformative potential of information technology in library and information science.
Six multi-year projects were funded in the first four years of the DLI, involving collaborations from various organizations.
Paul Evan Peters posited the term 'digital library' as a replacement for the terms 'electronic library' and 'virtual library' in 1995.
Initial thinking about digital libraries for science education began in 1995 with an internal concept paper for the NSF Division of Undergraduate Education (DUE).
The concepts for digital libraries were developed through a series of workshops and reports from 1998 to 1999.
By fiscal year 1998, the initial Digital Libraries Initiative (DLI) had gained more partner agencies.

The paper 'For a clever country: information literacy diffusion in the 21st century' is authored by Alana Bundy.
The paper serves as a background and issues document for the first national roundtable on information literacy organized by the Australian Library and Information Association (ALIA).
The roundtable was held at the State Library of Victoria on 28 February 2001.
Information literacy is defined as an understanding and set of abilities that enable individuals to recognize when information is needed and to identify, locate, evaluate, and use that information effectively.
An information literate person can recognize a need for information, determine the extent of information needed, access information efficiently, evaluate information and its sources, and incorporate selected information into their knowledge base.
An information literate person can also use information effectively to accomplish a purpose, understand economic, legal, social, and cultural issues in the use of information, access and use information ethically and legally, and classify, store, manipulate, and redraft information.
Information literacy is necessary due to the proliferation of information access and resources.
Individuals encounter diverse and abundant information choices in their studies, workplaces, and lives.
Information is available from various sources, including community resources, special interest organizations, manufacturers, service providers, media, libraries, and the internet.
The increasing availability of unfiltered information raises questions about authenticity, validity, and reliability.

The ERIC Digest is authored by Brandy Schuman.
The digest discusses the concept of filial therapy.
Many children do not have their need for emotional nurturing met according to Landreth (2002).
Communication gaps between parents and children may exist because many parents are unaware of their children's emotional needs and lack the skills necessary to interact effectively with them on an emotional level according to Landreth (2002).
Children communicate through play, which is their innate language according to Axline (1969) and Landreth (2002).
Teaching parents the language of play and how to use play therapeutically can close the communication gap between parent and child according to Guerney, Guerney, & Andronico (1999) and Landreth (2002).
Filial therapy is an alternative method for treating emotionally disturbed children in which the parent is used as an ally in the therapeutic process.
In filial therapy, the parent becomes the child's primary therapeutic agent according to Guerney et al. (1999), Landreth (2000), and VanFleet (2000).
Parental involvement in a child's developmental process facilitates the parent's motivation to continue therapy sessions.
Parental involvement tends to eliminate typical parental resistance encountered when the parent is not involved in the child's therapy.

Duct tape is more effective for treating warts than liquid nitrogen or topical anti-wart cream.
To treat a wart with duct tape, cut the tape to the size of the wart.
The duct tape should be left on the wart for 6 days.
If the duct tape falls off during the 6 days, a new piece should be applied.
On the seventh day, the tape should be removed and the affected area soaked in water for half an hour.
After soaking, the wart should be gently debrided with an emory board or pumice stone.
A new piece of duct tape should be applied after debriding the wart.
This process should be repeated until the wart is gone.

An analysis by Warren et al. (2000) found no evidence that working during high school affected academic grades in the short or long term.

A study in monkeys suggests that the brain plays a significant role in the decision to mate.
Researchers at the University of Wisconsin-Madison conducted brain scans of marmoset monkeys.
The study used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to examine brain functions in Brazilian monkeys.
The researchers observed high levels of neural activity in areas of the brain important for decision-making and sexual arousal when the monkeys smelled certain scents.
Psychology professor Charles Snowdon noted that areas associated with decision-making, memory, emotional processing, reward, and cognitive control showed unexpected levels of activity.
Common marmosets live in family groups and do not mate freely, requiring careful mate selection.
The study involved four male marmosets and gland secretion samples from females at or near ovulation.
The researchers found that the monkeys' brains showed more activity when smelling samples from fertile females compared to non-fertile females.
This study is the first to image an awake nonhuman primate in response to emotionally arousing stimuli.
The marmoset data corresponded closely to human fMRI studies.

El ERIC Digest titulado 'El estres y los ninos pequenos' está en español.
Este Digest es una traducción de 'Stress and Young Children'.
Históricamente, el estrés se ha definido en relación con su origen, tanto interno como externo.
Los orígenes internos del estrés incluyen hambre, dolor, sensibilidad a ruidos, cambios de temperatura, congestión de personas, cansancio y exceso o falta de estimulación del ambiente físico inmediato.
Los factores estresantes externos incluyen separación de la familia, cambios en la composición familiar, exposición a disputas y conflictos interpersonales, violencia, agresión de otros, pérdida de propiedad personal importante o de una mascota, expectativas excesivas respecto al logro, 'andar de prisa' y desorganización de eventos cotidianos.
La literatura de investigación a menudo se enfoca en el impacto de factores estresantes de una sola variable en el desarrollo de niños.
En situaciones de la vida real, los niños experimentan estrés de orígenes múltiples.
Los investigadores observan que los factores estresantes múltiples interactúan entre sí y pueden tener efectos cumulativos.
Este Digest discute cómo los niños experimentan y se adaptan al estrés.
El Digest ofrece sugerencias a maestros y padres sobre cómo prevenir y reducir el estrés infantil.

Thrombotic strokes occur when a vessel clots off, also preventing downstream tissue from receiving oxygen.
Embolic strokes occur when a piece of matter breaks off and lodges in a smaller vessel, stopping blood flow to that area of the brain.
There are treatments available for thrombotic and embolic strokes.

A 52-year-old woman discovered that two of her three sons were biologically unrelated to her.

The woman's mother likely conceived non-identical twin girls who fused early in pregnancy.
Cells from only one twin dominate in the woman's blood, while both twins' cells exist in her other tissues.
One of the woman's sons came from an egg of the dominant twin, while the other two sons came from the other twin's eggs.

This Digest examines the limited research available on the social group's role in bullying to understand how bullying and victimization may emerge or continue during early adolescence.

El recreo en la escuela primaria es definido por Pellegrini y Smith (1993) como un tiempo de descanso para los niños, típicamente fuera del edificio.
Durante el recreo, los niños disfrutan de más libertad para escoger qué hacer y con quién.
Una encuesta de 1989 realizada por la National Association of Elementary School Principals encontró que el 90% de los distritos tenía escuelas con al menos un periodo de recreo durante el día.
La American Association for the Child's Right to Play indica que muchos distritos escolares han abolido el recreo desde 1989.
Las preocupaciones de seguridad y responsabilidad legal, así como el temor de que el recreo interrumpa las rutinas de trabajo, podrían ser razones para eliminar el recreo.
Otro motivo citado para eliminar el recreo es la necesidad de pasar más tiempo en la instrucción.
Directores y maestros han expresado que se sienten bajo presión para llenar el día escolar con instrucción debido a nuevas demandas de responsabilidad.
Es importante conocer lo que la investigación indica sobre el recreo, especialmente en el contexto de decisiones educativas basadas en la investigación.

There is no chemical bonding or reaction between a pressure-sensitive adhesive and the substrate.
A pressure-sensitive adhesive is a sticky, viscous, liquidlike material that adheres to a surface using only pressure.
Good adhesion requires the adhesive to have good cohesion and the ability to flow out on the surface.
The degree of flow of the adhesive affects the intensity of adhesion.
The degree of flow depends on the difference between the surface energy of the material and the surface energy of the adhesive.
Pressure-sensitive adhesives tend to flow out on materials with high surface energy, such as metals, glass, and certain plastics.
Pressure-sensitive adhesives do not flow out easily on low surface-energy materials like polyethylene, polypropylene, and Teflon.
Adhesion mechanisms include mechanical adhesion and specific adhesion.
Mechanical adhesion occurs when the adhesive flows into the texture of the substrate.
Specific adhesion includes electrostatic forces, van der Waals forces, and acid-base interactions between the adhesive and the substrate.

Maple Syrup Urine Disease is an inheritable metabolic disease of amino acid metabolism.

In the most severe form, Maple Syrup Urine Disease causes severe acidosis during the first week of life.
Symptoms of severe Maple Syrup Urine Disease include progressively poorer feeding, vomiting, seizures, lethargy, and coma.
Untreated infants with severe forms of Maple Syrup Urine Disease may die in the first few weeks of life.
Maple Syrup Urine Disease can also occur in intermittent and mild forms.
Even in mild forms, Maple Syrup Urine Disease can result in mental retardation and bouts of acidosis.

Goiter results in a visibly enlarged lower neck area.

The thyroid is influenced by environmental factors and dietary minerals, particularly iodine.
Dietary iodine is primarily obtained from ocean vegetables, ocean fish, and foods grown in iodine-rich soil.
Areas with over-farmed or geologically old soil may lack sufficient iodine.
Euthyroid goiter can occur during periods of significant hormonal changes, such as puberty, pregnancy, and menopause.

The ERIC Digest is authored by Alice Honig.
The digest reviews research on quality in infant-toddler programs.
Quality in infant-toddler programs is measured by structural and process variables.
Structural variables include space, number of babies per caregiver, and group size.
Process variables include the richness of 'turn-taking-talk' and warmth between caregivers and babies.
Fenichel and colleagues identified eight aspects of high-quality infant care.
The eight aspects include health and safety, small groups, primary caregiver assignment, continuity of care, caregiver responsivity, meeting individual needs, cultural sensitivity, and a stimulating physical environment.
The NCCSS study reported an average annual caregiver turnover rate of 41% across participating centers.

Some recent studies have been experimental, involving random assignment of children and families to groups that do or do not attend programs.
Experimental studies provide the most unequivocal evidence of the effects of preschool programs.
Other recent studies have been quasi-experimental, involving groups that do not attend programs without random assignment or a comparison group.
Quasi-experimental studies do not completely refute alternative explanations but allow examination of evidence in situations where experimental design was impossible.

The ERIC Digest titled 'Trends in Community College Financing: Challenges of the Past, Present, and Future' is authored by Linda Strauss.
The digest examines the history and future of community college funding.
Community colleges face challenges in generating sufficient revenue to fulfill their missions.
Many community colleges originated as extensions of secondary schools funded by public school budgets.
In 1918, local funds accounted for 94% of community college income.
The initial funding model for community colleges became insufficient, leading to the inclusion of state revenue, tuition and fees, federal funds, and gifts and grants.
By the 1960s, state appropriations became the primary source of revenue for community colleges, making up 34% of their income.
Individual states exhibit variations in the percentage of funding from state appropriations.
During the 1980s, there was a shift in funding sources away from state and local support.
In 1980, state support for community colleges was 70%, which decreased to 50% by 1996.

Bit rot, also known as bit decay, is a hypothetical disease inferred from the observation that unused programs or features may stop working over time.
The theory of bit rot suggests that bits decay similarly to radioactive materials.

There are physical processes that can cause such effects, including alpha particles from trace radionuclides in ceramic chip packages.
These physical processes can unpredictably change the contents of computer memory and may corrupt files in mass storage.
Such physical processes are rare, and computers are designed with error-detecting circuitry to mitigate their effects.
The belief that cosmic rays cause bit rot is a myth.
Software rot is nearly synonymous with bit rot, where software rot refers to the effect and bit rot refers to the notional cause.

The ERIC Digest titled 'English Language Learners and High-Stakes Tests: An Overview of the Issues' is authored by Bronwyn Coltrane.
The digest discusses factors to consider when making decisions about English Language Learners (ELLs) and high-stakes tests.
Tests used for high-stakes assessment must reflect the curriculum and standards of the state or district.
Menken (2000) states that effective assessments must be closely aligned with classroom teaching and learning driven by standards.
When tests are aligned with standards and curricula, students have a better chance of demonstrating their knowledge and abilities.
Teachers of ELLs should be involved in the decision-making process for selecting appropriate tests.
Testing committees at various levels should include teachers who work with ELLs to ensure test appropriateness.
Educators must consider appropriate testing accommodations for individual students or groups of students.
Translation of a test into a student's native language may benefit ELLs with strong cognitive-academic proficiency in that language.
Accommodations may include changes in how tests are presented and how students respond, as well as modifications related to timing and setting.

The Capability Maturity Model for Software (CMM) is a model for assessing the maturity of an organization's software processes.
A process in this context encompasses all operations related to software projects from proposal to project closure.
Processes are sequential and may include parallel operations across various Key Process Areas (KPAs).
CMM identifies five levels of process maturity.
Each level reflects the evolution of the process in terms of its maturity and capability to handle variations.
The first level is 'Initial', where the organization lacks a defined process.
The second level is 'Repeatable', where some best practices are followed, but processes are not standardized across all projects.
At level three, organizations have a defined Organization Defined Software Process (ODSP) that is flexible enough for various projects.
From the ODSP, a Project Defined Software Process (PDSP) is tailored for specific projects.
Level three involves defining a process, which includes creating templates and guidelines for handling KPAs and maintaining traceability.

CFP - Information Literacy is seeking manuscripts for the Winter 2004 issue of Academic Exchange Quarterly.
Elizabeth Blakesley Lindsay is the feature editor for the topic of information literacy.
Information literacy has transformed many library instruction programs into broader collaborative efforts.
The focus of the issue includes the use of information resources, identification of information needs, evaluation of information, ethical use of materials, and awareness of economic, legal, and social issues regarding information use.
The issue will examine theoretical and practical approaches for transforming library instruction programs into information literacy programs.
The issue will address fostering collaboration between librarians and faculty, defining and implementing information literacy competencies and standards, and examining models and methods of instruction.
Topics include teaching information literacy via distance education and debates over integrating information literacy into the curriculum versus delivering skills through a credit course.
The assessment of information literacy skills will also be addressed in the issue.
Librarians and faculty who have designed, taught, or assessed information literacy programs are invited to submit manuscripts.
The regular submission deadline is any time until the end of August 2004, with accepted submissions published in the Winter issue in December.

Two Truths And A Lie is a popular orientation game.

A third issue is providing overly specific statements that others may not care about.
An example of overly specific statements is: 'I had a fish named Scooter when I was six years old', 'I had a dog named Spot when I was nine years old', 'I had a cat named Betsy when I was twelve years old'.
